title.en: Give an invented creature a consistent body plan

summary: Fix limb count, joint axes, mass distribution and sensory orientation once, then let style exaggerate them.
objective: Make an invented creature read as a single organism whose movement follows from its construction.
applies_when: A non-existing creature, mascot or fictional animal is being designed.
A creature already moves but reads as an assembly of parts.
Several creatures must belong to the same fictional world.
intent_signals: invent a creature for the garden
the creature looks like random parts
example_prompts: Design a six-legged garden creature that moves like it is built that way.
Make the flying creature look capable of carrying its own weight.
negative_signals: Deliberately incoherent or surreal designs where impossible anatomy is the point.
Real animals, where anatomy is a factual matter requiring sources.
not_for: Deliberately incoherent or surreal designs where impossible anatomy is the point.
Real animals, where anatomy is a factual matter requiring sources.

principles: Coherence, not realism, is what makes an invented creature convincing: repeated limb structure, a consistent joint direction and a plausible relationship between mass and support.
Joints are the strongest signal. A limb whose segments bend in alternating directions reads as a leg; a limb whose joints bend arbitrarily reads as a tentacle or as an error.
Support must match mass. A heavy body on thin distal limbs needs a visible reason such as a broad foot, a counterbalancing tail or a suspended posture.
Sensors and mouth parts set the front of the creature and therefore its turning behaviour and resting orientation.
implementation: Decide the plan explicitly: number of limbs, segments per limb, joint axes and their directions, symmetry, tail or counterweight, and where the sensory end is.
Repeat the same joint logic across limb pairs, then vary length and thickness by role, such as digging forelimbs and springing hind limbs.

For a grounded creature, declare the support model and place the centre of mass over the support polygon in the rest pose and in the quasi-static poses it will hold. Flying, swimming, climbing and transient dynamic poses are outside that test and need their own justification, such as lift, adhesion or momentum.
Add style at the surface, in scale relationships and in silhouette, after the plan is fixed, so exaggeration does not invalidate the mechanics.
Where several creatures share a world, reuse the plan with variations so they read as related species.
observable_checks: For the poses the creature actually holds on the ground, project the centre of mass and check it lies within the declared support polygon. A failure says the pose is not statically balanced under that model, which may be intended for a lunge or a fall; it does not by itself establish that the design is unbuildable, and it does not apply to flight or other unsupported poses.
Compare limb pairs: joints that bend in inconsistent directions between left and right are almost always mistakes.
Show only the silhouette and ask which end is the front; ambiguity here usually means the sensory end is undefined.
Play the intended motion at half speed and look for limbs whose range exceeds what their joints allow.

creative_affordances: Asymmetry, extra limbs, impossible proportions and non-biological materials are all legitimate once the plan is deliberate.
A creature may violate its own plan for a story reason, such as an injury or a prosthesis, when that is visible in the design.
known_limits: Authored creative guidance for invented creatures; it asserts no biological or biomechanical fact.
Real-animal anatomy, gait energetics and load capacity require sourced research rather than this rule.
